senses.def: pertaining to one for whom there is no record of ancestors
an abundant amount, with the implication of generosity

senses.subdomain: Indefinite Units of Time: Age, Lifetime, Interval, Period
senses.def: a unit of time as a particular stage or period of history
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no specific term for ‘age’ or ‘era.’ The closest approximation in the context of Matthew 12:32 may be ‘not in these many years and not in the many years which will follow.’|In 1 Timothy 1:17 (τῷ δὲ βασιλεῖ τῶν αἰώνων literally ‘to the king of the ages’) the genitive phrase τῶν αἰώνων is better understood as an abstract of unlimited extent of time, and accordingly, one may translate more accurately as ‘the eternal king.’ Compare 67.95.

senses.def: the universe, perhaps with some associated meaning of ‘eon’ or ‘age’ in the sense of the transitory nature of the universe (but this is doubtful in the contexts of Hebrews 1:2 and Hebrews 11:3)
senses.comment: In Hebrews 1:2 it may be essential in a number of languages to translate ‘he is the one through whom God created everything,’ though in some instances a more idiomatic and satisfactory way of rendering the meaning would involve a phrase such as ‘… created both the earth and the sky’ or ‘… the heavens and the earth.’

senses.def: the system of practices and standards associated with secular society (that is, without reference to any demands or requirements of God)
senses.comment: αἰών in 1 Corinthians 3:18 may also be rendered as ‘by the way in which people in this world think’ or ‘by the things which people in this world think are right.’ In Mark 4:19 the phrase αἱ μέριμναι τοῦ αἰῶνος may be rendered as ‘the cares which people in this world have’ or ‘the way in which people in this world worry about things.’

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Other Points of Time: Before, Long Ago, Now, At the Same Time, When, About, After
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: from an age) a point of time preceding another point of time, with a very long interval between (more emphatic than πάλαι[a], ἔκπαλαι[a], 67.24)
senses.comment: Some persons have concluded that ἀπ᾽ αἰῶνος must be understood in the sense of ‘from an earlier age,’ but there seems to be no justification for reading a dispensational implication into this idiomatic expression.

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time with Reference to Some Point of Time: Until, Delay, Still, From
senses.def: an exceedingly long period of time from an assumed beginning up to the present

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: unlimited duration of time, with particular focus upon the future
senses.comment: See also Luke 1:33; 2 Peter 3:18; Jude 1:25; Hebrews 1:8. The more elaborate expressions employing αἰών are somewhat more emphatic in meaning and are to be found especially in the solemn style of doxologies.

senses.def: title for supernatural forces and powers: a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
senses.comment: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.

senses.def: (a title for the Devil, literally: the god of this world) one who has power or authority over this world (or this age) and is so recognized by people of the world
senses.comment: The expression ‘the god of this world’ may be understood in two senses: (1) the god who rules over this world or (2) the god whom the people of this world trust or worship. Though many persons have traditionally interpreted ‘the god of this world’ as the one who rules over this world, it is the second meaning which probably fits more accurately in the context of 2 Corinthians 4:4.

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: sons of this age) persons who hold to the value system of the world
senses.comment: In some instances ‘the people of this world’ may be rendered as ‘the people who live like most people in the world’ or ‘the people who are concerned only about what people say.’ Sometimes the identification with the world is expressed in contrast with people’s attitude concerning God, for example, ‘people who have no use for God.’

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: yesterday, today, and forever) an unlimited extension of time, from the past into the future
(a causative derivative of ἅλς ‘salt,’ 5.25) to cause something to taste salty
glosses: to restore the flavor to salt
senses.comment: In Matthew 5:13 one may employ a causative such as ‘how will the salt be made salty again’ or ‘how can one cause the salt to return.’ In Mark 9:49 the meaning is particularly obscure. According to OT requirements sacrifices were to be salted (), and it may be that in Mark 9:49 the fire is regarded as an equivalent of salt and as a symbol of suffering and sacrifice by which the disciple is tested.

senses.def: a circular net with weights and a draw rope around its edge; used in fishing
senses.comment: An ἀμφίβληστρον had small weights attached to the outer border, and it was normally thrown in such a manner as to encircle fish. In trying to obtain a satisfactory equivalent expression in another language, it is not necessary to try to duplicate all the details of form. What is important is that such a net was thrown rather than being dragged.

senses.def: to destroy, with the possible implication of something being used up
senses.comment: In contexts such as Luke 9:54 it is always possible to translate a term such as ἀναλίσκω as ‘to cause to die.’

senses.def: air in relatively rapid movement, but without specification as to the force of the movement
senses.comment: As in the case of English (which has, for example, such terms as breeze, zephyr, gust, storm, whirlwind, cyclone, tornado, etc.), other languages likewise normally have a number of different terms depending upon the strength of the wind and whether the wind may be carrying substances such as sand or dust. In some languages there may also be a problem involved in the use of terms for ‘wind,’ since some of these may have meanings of malicious or malevolent spirits, or they may imply a disease-bringing event.

senses.def: the ability or capacity to help or assist
to be determined to avoid doing something
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀπεῖπον in 2 Corinthians 4:2, see 33.220.

senses.def: to assert opposition to something
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀπεῖπον in 2 Corinthians 4:2, see 13.156.

senses.def: to cause a state, with focus upon the process
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἀποκυέω ‘to give birth to,’ not occurring in the NT) to be brought into being as something newly created
to use force in pushing or thrusting someone or something away or aside
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἀπωθέω[a] ‘to push away,’ 15.46) to no longer pay attention to previous beliefs

senses.subdomain: Duration of Time without Reference to Points or Units of Time: Time, Spend Time, Always, Eternal, Old, Immediately, Young
senses.def: pertaining to having existed for a long time in the past, with the possible implication of such existence from the beginning of an event or state

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to act in defiance of social and moral standards, with resulting disgrace, embarrassment, and shame
senses.comment: Behavior involving disgrace, embarrassment, and shame is often expressed in an idiomatic manner, for example, ‘to bury one’s face,’ ‘to hide one’s eyes,’ or ‘to feel stabbed by people’s eyes.’ Since shame is seemingly a universal type of feeling, there is usually no difficulty involved in obtaining a satisfactory equivalent.

senses.def: pertaining to being without fear
senses.comment: An adverb such as ἀφόβως often corresponds to a clause in other languages. Accordingly, ‘dare to preach the message fearlessly’ must be rendered in some languages as ‘dare to preach the message without being afraid of anyone.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: pertaining to disgraceful behavior which shows no regard or fear for social sanctions
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ἀφόβως in Jude 1:12, see ἀφόβως[c] 53.60.

senses.def: pertaining to being without reverence or awe for God
senses.comment: It is also possible that ἀφόβως in Jude 1:12 should be understood as simply ‘being without fear’ or ‘boldly’ (25.253). For another interpretation of ἀφόβως in Jude 1:12, see ἀφόβως[b] 88.151.

senses.def: one who has absolute authority within a particular area and is able to convey this power and authority to a successor (though in NT times, certain kings ruled only with the approval of Roman authorities and had no power to pass on their prerogatives)
to speak against someone in such a way as to harm or injure his or her reputation (occurring in relation to persons as well as to divine beings)
senses.comment: One way in which βλασφημέω and βλασφημία[a] were used in speaking of defaming God was by claiming some kind of equality with God. Any such statement was regarded by the Jews of biblical times as being harmful and injurious to the nature of God.

senses.def: (derivative of βλασφημέω ‘to blaspheme,’ (33.400) the content of a defamation
white fluid secreted by women and female mammals for nourishment of their young; also used as food for humans
senses.comment: The term γάλα may refer to any type of milk, whether produced by humans or by certain domesticated animals, for example, cow, sheep, goat, camel.|In a number of languages two distinct terms are used for milk, one identifying the human milk and another term specifying milk from animals. In the context of 1 Corinthians 3:2 it is probably the latter reference which is important, though the passage is highly figurative and the emphasis is upon food for babies.

senses.def: to express one’s discontent
to eat a meal, without reference to any particular time of the day or to the type of food involved
senses.comment: In some languages it is impossible to speak of ‘having a meal’ without indicating the time of day or the nature of the food consumed.

senses.def: a type of crown employed as a symbol of the highest ruling power in a particular area and therefore often associated with kingship
senses.comment: In the NT διάδημα occurs only in Revelation 12:3, and such a crown may be described as ‘symbol of his power, worn on his head.’

senses.def: to keep oneself from doing something, with the implication of duration
to cause a quantity to be twice as much
glosses: to cause twice as much as

senses.def: west (as the direction of the setting sun)
senses.comment: In most languages east and west are related to the rising or setting sun, although in some languages there may be some local geographical feature which serves as a marker of direction, for example, the location of a particular mountain, the ocean, or a river. For north, some languages employ ‘to the left of the rising sun,’ that is to say, the direction is oriented in terms of the left hand of a person facing toward the rising sun. Similarly, south would be ‘to the right of the rising sun.’

senses.domain: Groups and Classes of Persons and Members of Such Groups and Classes
senses.def: (derivative of ἔθνος ‘nation,’ 11.55) pertaining to being like or similar to one who is not a Jew
senses.comment: In Galatians 2:14 one cannot use some such expression as ‘like those who do not believe in God’ (compare τὰ ἔθνη, 11.37), since here the contrast is between two types of believers, Jews and non-Jews. Frequently there is no specific term for ‘Gentile’ in contrast with Jews, and therefore it may be important to speak of ‘Gentiles’ as ‘those who are not Jews.’ Galatians 2:14 may then be rendered as ‘you are a Jew, but you have been living like those who are not Jews.’

senses.def: to expect something to happen, often implying waiting
senses.comment: The closest equivalent of ‘to expect’ is usually ‘to think that it will happen that.’

senses.def: sixth in a series involving either time, space, or set
to put or throw into a place
senses.comment: Despite the use of the verb ἐμβάλλω in Luke 12:5, the focus of meaning is not so much upon the act of throwing or hurling but rather upon the act of causing someone to be in a particular place.

senses.def: to enclose an object by winding something about or around it

senses.subdomain: Application and Removal of Liquids or Masses
senses.def: to remove a liquid by wiping off
(a figurative extension of meaning of ἐξαλείφω[a] ‘to wipe off, to wipe away,’ 47.18) to cause something to cease by obliterating any evidence
pertaining to being necessary and indispensable to the occurrence of some event

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.def: to sit down upon something
senses.comment: In Matthew 21:7 the pronominal form αὐτῶν is ambiguous in reference, for it may refer either to the garments or to the donkey and colt. The closest noun reference is τὰ ἱμάτια ‘the garments,’ but in view of Matthew’s quotation and evident interpretation of the reference to, both the donkey and the colt may be the substantive referents, though being seated upon two animals at the same time poses real problems of understanding.

senses.def: to do something with persistence, implying both continuity and strong effort
a person in the genealogy of Jesus
a Christian woman in the church of Philippi
the father of the apostles James and John
a degree which is lower than what would be expected in the context
pertaining to being less satisfactory than something else
(derivative of θεωρέω[a] ‘to observe,’ 24.14) an unusual object or event which is observed
a person who has not acquired systemic information or expertise in some field of knowledge or activity
senses.comment: In 1 Corinthians 14:16 ἰδιώτης is used to refer to a class of persons who were neither unbelievers nor fully instructed Christians, but who were inquirers or catechumens. In such a context, ἰδιώτης may be rendered as ‘ordinary, uninitiated’ (ἐπεὶ ἐὰν εὐλογῇς ἐν πνεύματι, ὁ ἀναπληρῶν τὸν τόπον τοῦ ἰδιώτου πῶς ἐρεῖ τὸ Ἀμήν ἐπὶ τῇ σῇ εὐχαριστίᾳ ‘when you give thanks to God in spirit only, how can an ordinary, uninitiated person taking part in the meeting say “Amen” to your prayer of thanksgiving’).

senses.def: an identifying name (probably based on a place name; see 93.496) of Judas, the betrayer of Jesus (Mark 3:19 and Mark 3:19, apparatus)
a marker of similarity in events and states, with the possible implication of something being in accordance with something else

senses.subdomain: Up To, As Much As, To the Degree That [Marked Extent of Degree]
senses.def: in accordance with a degree as specified by the context
senses.comment: There may be a number of problems of restructuring in rendering the relationship between clauses marked by καθό[b], καθώς[a], and καθότι[b]. For example, in the case of 1 Peter 4:13 it may be necessary to translate ‘how much you share Christ’s sufferings is how much you can rejoice.’

senses.def: to produce fruit or seed (of plants)
to cause results to exist
to witness against someone or some statement
to do something with success and/or thoroughness
a marker of an agent relation with numerable events, with the probable implication of comprehensiveness
to cause a state to be
to cause to be thoroughly prepared
to beat someone on the head, implying repeated blows
the state of being asleep
senses.comment: In some languages sleep is expressed by an idiom, for example, ‘his soul had wandered away’ or ‘his eyes had disappeared.’ Though an expression such as ‘his soul had wandered away’ might appear in some languages to have misleading theological implications, it really means only ‘to sleep.’

senses.def: (figurative extension of meaning of κοιμάομαι[a] ‘to sleep,’ 23.66) to sleep, as a euphemistic expression for the state of being dead
senses.comment: Some translators have attempted to preserve the figure of speech in καθεύδω[b] and κοιμάομαι[b] by translating ‘to sleep’ rather than ‘to have died’ or ‘to be dead.’ Such a practice, however, has resulted in misunderstanding in a number of instances and has sometimes led to the doctrine of so-called ‘soul-sleep.’

senses.def: (derivative of κράτος[a] ‘power,’ 76.6) pertaining to being powerful or mighty
senses.comment: In 1 Peter 5:6 χεῖρ is, of course, to be interpreted as power (see 76.3).

senses.def: (derivative of κύριος[c] ‘one who rules,’ 37.51) a supernatural ruling power
senses.comment: In general, the series of terms θρόνοι, κυριότητες, ἀρχαί, and ἐξουσίαι in Colossians 1:16 (as well as in Ephesians 1:21) are understood as being supernatural cosmic powers, whether angelic or demonic (see 12.44), but it is possible that these should be understood in terms of human rulers.

senses.def: (title for supernatural forces and powers) a supernatural power having some particular role in controlling the destiny and activities of human beings
senses.comment: Some scholars have believed that it is possible to reconstruct at least in part some of the hierarchy represented by these various supernatural forces and powers, on the basis of the neoplatonic system of nine such powers arranged in three orders of three each. NT terminology and usage does not, however, lend itself to such a classification, and it is difficult, if not impossible, to determine what are the significant differences between these supernatural powers and forces.|In the case of Ephesians 1:21 some scholars apply the terms in question both to the supernatural and to the human sphere, thus emphasizing the totality of Christ’s rule. This has a considerable measure of justification in view of the concepts held by persons in the ancient world, since various earthly powers were supposed to reflect corresponding supernatural powers.|For the most part, translators have endeavored to render the various terms in somewhat different ways, for example, ἐξουσία as ‘authority’; δύναμις as ‘power’; κυριότης as ‘ruler’; and phrases such as τὰ πνευματικὰ τῆς πονηρίας ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις as ‘wicked spiritual forces in the heavenly world.’ In a number of languages, however, there are simply not enough terms to designate various kinds of powers, authorities, and forces which could be employed in speaking of such supernatural impersonal powers. Accordingly, some translators have simply used a phrase such as ‘any and all kinds of supernatural powers.’ Where it is possible to make certain lexical distinctions between terms and phrases, this, of course, should be done, but in a number of contexts this may be impossible, and accordingly, some explanation in a marginal note may be required if the reader is to understand satisfactorily the intent of the passages in question.

senses.def: to not recall information and thus to lose sight of its significance
senses.comment: In a number of languages the fact of ‘forgetting’ or ‘not remembering’ is expressed idiomatically, for example, ‘to lose out of one’s heart,’ ‘to have one’s thoughts walk away,’ or ‘to have words disappear from one’s liver.’

senses.def: the grandmother of Timothy
to beat severely with a whip
a wall or fence which separates one area from another
senses.comment: In the NT μεσότοιχον is used figuratively in reference to the partition in the Temple in Jerusalem, which set off the court of the Gentiles from the rest of the Temple area.|Such a ‘dividing wall’ may be rendered as ‘barrier’ or ‘fence which separates.’

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: to cause someone to be morally tainted or defiled
glosses: to cause to be morally filthy

senses.def: to cause something to be ceremonially impure, with the implication of serious defilement
cardinal number, where there are ten thousand instances of a countable entity
a very large indefinite number

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of νήφω[b] ‘to be restrained,’ 88.86) pertaining to behaving in a sober, restrained manner
senses.comment: In a number of languages νηφάλιος may be idiomatically rendered as ‘one who holds himself in’ or ‘one who always has a halter on himself.’

senses.def: cardinal number, where there are eighty instances of a countable entity
pertaining to being whole, complete, or entire, with focus on unity
a totality as a complete unit
a degree of totality or completeness
to eagerly desire to accomplish some goal or purpose
(a technical, nautical term) to sail up to or near
to think or reason in a completely irrational manner
glosses: to not be in one’s right mind
to be out of one’s mind

senses.def: a city on the southwest coast of the island of Cyprus
pertaining to being very sad or deeply distressed
to fall from one level to another
to fall from a standing or upright position down to the ground or surface

senses.domain: Stances and Events Related to Stances
senses.subdomain: Prostrate as an Act of Reverence or Supplication
senses.def: to prostrate oneself before someone, implying supplication
senses.comment: A strictly literal translation of προσπίπτω[a] or πίπτω[c], namely, to fall down before, can be entirely misleading in that it may suggest an accident caused by stumbling or tripping. It may therefore be necessary in a number of languages to translate to bow down low before or to bow down to the ground before.

senses.def: to suffer or experience destruction
(a figurative extension of meaning of πίπτω[a] ‘to fall,’ 15.118) to fall down, as a euphemistic expression for a violent death
senses.comment: It is rare that one can employ a literal meaning of πίπτω as a euphemistic expression for ‘dying,’ since receptors are too likely to understand ‘to fall’ in a purely literal sense.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of πίπτω[a] ‘to fall,’ 15.118) to cease, with the possible implication of failure
senses.comment: For another interpretation of πίπτω in 1 Corinthians 13:8, see 75.7.

senses.def: to happen suddenly to, with the connotation of something bad and adverse
senses.comment: In this particular context it may be necessary to be somewhat more specific concerning the blindness that Elymas experienced. For example, one may render this expression as ‘suddenly a dark mist covered his eyes’ or ‘suddenly the eyes of Elymas became dark and misty’ (see 24.40).

senses.def: to change for the worse, with emphasis upon extent and suddenness
to cease to exist in a particular post or position
(figurative extension of meaning of πίπτω[a] ‘to fall,’ 15.118) to become inadequate for some function
senses.comment: For another interpretation of πίπτω in 1 Corinthians 13:8, see 68.49.

senses.def: to experience somewhat suddenly that which is difficult or bad

senses.subdomain: To Choose, To Select, To Prefer
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: the lot falls upon someone) the process of choosing, with the probable implication of discerning God’s will in this manner
senses.comment: In some societies the closest natural equivalents of deciding by lot are procedures involving ‘drawing straws’ or ‘throwing dice’ or ‘throwing down sticks’ or ‘dropping pebbles.’

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to fall upon someone) to cause someone suffering or harm
senses.comment: It is rare indeed that this idiom can ever be produced literally in other languages, though it may be possible to preserve some of the figurative impact by translating ‘nor will the heat of the sun ever cause them to suffer.’

senses.subdomain: High Status or Rank [including persons of high status]
senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to his own master he stands or falls, probably a familiar adage) whether one maintains one’s status or relationship to a master depends on the masters judgment or evaluation
glosses: honor or disgrace depends on the person whom one serves

senses.def: (an idiom, literally: to fall under judgment) to be condemned for acting contrary to laws and regulations
senses.comment: In the context of James 5:12 the condemnation refers to God’s judgment.

senses.def: to herd and tend flocks of sheep or goats
senses.comment: In a number of cultures sheep are not herded or taken care of; they serve primarily as scavengers, and therefore it may be necessary to introduce some type of marginal note, especially in passages which have figurative significance.

senses.def: (a figurative extension of meaning of ποιμαίνω[a] ‘to shepherd,’ 44.3) to lead, with the implication of providing for
glosses: to guide and take care of

senses.def: to rule, with the implication of direct personal involvement
activities involved in one’s behavior or conduct
senses.comment: In some languages it is possible to translate ‘in the affairs of daily life’ as ‘in what most people must do every day.’

senses.def: to change one’s state for the better by advancing and making progress
to be terrified as the result of something which startles or alarms
the event of destruction, involving splitting open and breaking
senses.comment: Though the noun ῥῆγμα with the derivative suffix μα might lead one to assume that the reference is to a state of ruin or destruction, the context points to the actual event of destruction, and therefore the translation of ‘crash’ or ‘destruction.’

senses.def: the Hebrew name of the apostle Paul
the first king of Israel

senses.subdomain: Cloth, Leather, and Objects Made of Such Materials
senses.def: linen cloth of good quality
senses.comment: In a number of languages there is no term for ‘linen,’ and though a word for ‘linen’ may be borrowed, what is important in the NT contexts in which σινδών occurs is primarily the quality of the cloth, not the material of which it was made. Accordingly, many translators have used an expression such as ‘fine cloth’ or ‘good cloth.’

senses.def: the capacity to understand and, as a result, to act wisely
the content of what is known by those regarded as wise
knowledge which makes possible skillful activity or performance
senses.comment: It is also possible to interpret σοφία in 1 Corinthians 1:17 as wisdom which makes possible correct understanding (see 32.32).

senses.def: a document or book containing wise sayings (as in the phrase ἡ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ ‘the Wisdom of God,’ Luke 11:49, a possible reference to the OT or to apocryphal wisdom literature, possibly even a book which has been lost)
senses.comment: If one understands ἡ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ as being a reference to a book, one could translate the statement in Luke 11:49 as ‘for this reason, the book entitled The Wisdom of God has the words: …’ On the other hand, the phrase ἡ σοφία τοῦ θεοῦ in Luke 11:49 may mean merely ‘God’s wisdom’ (32.32), and therefore this expression in Luke 11:49 could be rendered as ‘God in his wisdom said’ or ‘God, who is wise, said.’

senses.domain: Body, Body Parts, and Body Products
senses.def: a permanent mark or scar on the body, especially the type of brand used to mark ownership of slaves
senses.comment: In Galatians 6:17 Paul is most likely alluding to scars resulting from wounds received in the service of Jesus, but στίγμα may also imply ownership and hence suggest that such scars served as brands (see 8.56). For other interpretations of στίγμα in Galatians 6:17, see 33.481 and 90.84.

senses.def: something on the surface of an object, for example, line, spot, or scar, without special design but carrying significance
senses.comment: A strictly literal translation of Galatians 6:17 might suggest that Paul had the same marks on his hands, feet, and side as Jesus had, but this is evidently not the meaning of the state ment in Galatians 6:17. It is possible, of course, that since Paul was whipped much the same way that Jesus was whipped, he (Paul) would bear such scars on his back, but a more satisfactory rendering of Galatians 6:17 would probably be ‘for I have on my body scars indicating that I belong to Jesus.’ For other interpretations of στίγμα in Galatians 6:17, see 8.55 and 90.84.

senses.def: (derivative of συζητέω[a] ‘to debate, to dispute,’ 33.440) a person who is skilled in or likely to be involved in expressing strong differences of opinion
to cause to gather together (compare συναθροίζομαι, 15.130)
to assemble together, with emphasis on the element of togetherness (compare ἀθροίζω, 15.129)
to bring an activity to a successful finish
senses.comment: It is also possible to render this phrase in Romans 9:28 as ‘for he will settle the account,’ the implication being that he will accomplish what he has said he would do.

senses.def: to cause to exist by virtue of its having been finally accomplished

senses.subdomain: A Point of Time with Reference to Duration of Time: Beginning, End
senses.def: (derivative of συντέλεια ‘end,’ 67.66) to occur or happen at the end of a duration

senses.domain: Moral and Ethical Qualities and Related Behavior
senses.def: (derivative of the stem σωφρο ‘to behave in a sensible manner,’ 88.93) pertaining to being sensible and moderate in one’s behavior
senses.comment: In a number of languages terms such as σωφρονισμός[b] (88.93), σωφροσύνη[b] (88.93), σώφρων, and σωφρόνως may be rendered as ‘to have right thoughts about what one should do’ or ‘to let one’s mind guide one’s body.’

senses.subdomain: Definite Units of Time: Year, Month, Week, Day, Hour
senses.def: pertaining to a period of forty years
cardinal number, where there are three instances of a countable entity
a container for storing or carrying water or other liquids; made of stone or clay
pertaining to being subject to justifying behavior before a court of justice
the burning vapor surrounding an object on fire
senses.comment: As in the case of πῦρa ‘fire’ (2.3), the term φλόξ ‘flame’ is likewise frequently rendered by a verb rather than by a noun. Accordingly, in a passage such as Acts 7:30 ‘in the flames of a burning bush’ becomes ‘where the burning bush was flaming up’ or ‘where flames were burning a bush.’ In some languages ‘flames’ are referred to as ‘the tongues of the fire’ or ‘the banner of the fire.’ In a number of languages, however, no distinction is made between ‘fire’ and ‘flame.’

senses.def: to cause light to shine upon some object, in the sense of illuminating it
senses.comment: Expressions involving the causing of light to shine upon an object often involve explicit causative elements, for example, ‘to cause light to shine upon’ or ‘to cause to shine’ or ‘to cause to be bright’ or ‘to cause to be in the light.’

senses.def: to cause something to be fully known by revealing clearly and in some detail
small green plants (and in NT contexts referring primarily to green grass in a field or meadow)
senses.comment: In referring to small green plants, a number of languages employ two quite different terms, one indicating specifically grass (with leaves having parallel veins) and the other designating all other types of annual plants (those having branching veins in the leaves). In Matthew 13:26 it is important to employ a term which would include grass and other plants with parallel veins, since the weeds in this passage imitate the appearance of wheat, which does have parallel veins in the leaves.

senses.def: the young growth of a plant arising from a germinating seed
senses.comment: In a number of languages a clear distinction is made between different kinds of ‘sprouts.’ Certain sprouts have only a single blade (for example, grass), while others are double (as in the case of beans). In Mark 4:28 the reference is to a grass-like plant with a single blade

senses.def: pertaining to being material or physical, especially in relation to life processes
senses.comment: In some languages, however, it is impossible to translate σπείρεται in 1 Corinthians 15:44 as ‘sown,’ and one must therefore translate this expression as ‘when buried, it is a physical body.’

senses.def: pertaining to human nature (possibly contrasting with σάρκινος[c] and σαρκικός[c] ‘natural, human,’ 79.4, in focusing somewhat more on so-called higher endowments of personality)
senses.comment: For another interpretation of ψυχικός in 1 Corinthians 2:14, see 41.41.

senses.def: (derivative of ψυχή[a] ‘inner self,’ 26.4) pertaining to behavior which is typical of human nature, in contrast with that which is under the control of God’s Spirit
senses.comment: In a number of languages the equivalent of ‘unspiritual’ is simply ‘one who is not guided by God’s Spirit’ or ‘one who does not live in accordance with God’s Spirit.’ For another interpretation of ψυχικός in 1 Corinthians 2:14, see 79.5.
